calculations.title: Percentage change
formulas: % change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100
calculations.meaning: The building block of almost every IB calculation: elasticities, growth rates, inflation and exchange-rate changes all start from it.
calculations.tip: "New minus old, over OLD." Always divide by the starting value — never the new one.

practice.question: A value changes from {{f(old)}} to {{f(neu)}}. Calculate the percentage change.

calculations.title: Price elasticity of demand (PED)
formulas: PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP
calculations.meaning: How responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price. |PED| > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic, = 1 unit elastic.
calculations.tip: "Q on top" — quantity always goes in the numerator. PED is negative for normal demand, so quote its absolute value.

practice.question: When the price of a product {{s > 0 ? "rises" : "falls"}} from {{m(p1)}} to {{m(p2)}}, quantity demanded {{s > 0 ? "falls" : "rises"}} from {{q1}} to {{q2}} units a week. Calculate the PED and state whether demand is price elastic or price inelastic.
steps: |PED| = {{f(ped)}}, which is {{ped > 1 ? "greater" : "less"}} than 1, so demand is {{ped > 1 ? "price elastic" : "price inelastic"}}: quantity changes by a {{ped > 1 ? "larger" : "smaller"}} percentage than price.

calculations.title: PED and total revenue
formulas: TR = P × Q
ΔTR = TR after − TR before
calculations.meaning: Checks the PED–revenue rule: with elastic demand price and TR move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand they move together.
calculations.tip: "Elastic: opposite. Inelastic: in step." If price rises and TR rises, demand must be inelastic.

practice.question: A firm {{s > 0 ? "raises" : "cuts"}} its price from {{m(p1)}} to {{m(p2)}} and its sales change from {{q1}} to {{q2}} units. Calculate total revenue before and after, the change in total revenue, and say what this suggests about PED.
steps: Price {{s > 0 ? "rose" : "fell"}} and TR {{tr2 > tr1 ? "rose" : "fell"}}: {{(s > 0) === (tr2 > tr1) ? "they moved together, so demand is price inelastic" : "they moved in opposite directions, so demand is price elastic"}} (PED = {{f(ped)}}).

calculations.title: Income elasticity of demand (YED)
formulas: YED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔY
calculations.meaning: How demand responds to income. YED < 0 inferior; 0 < YED < 1 normal necessity; YED > 1 normal luxury.
calculations.tip: Keep the sign! Negative = inferior. Then "under 1 = need it, over 1 = luxury".

practice.question: Average household income rises from {{m(y1)}} to {{m(y2)}} a year, and quantity demanded of a good changes from {{q1}} to {{q2}} units. Calculate YED and classify the good.

parts.label: The good is
parts.answer: yed < 0 ? "an inferior good" : yed < 1 ? "a normal good (necessity)" : "a normal good (luxury)"

steps: {{yed < 0 ? "YED is negative, so demand falls as income rises: an inferior good." : yed < 1 ? "YED is positive but less than 1: a normal good and a necessity (income inelastic)." : "YED is greater than 1: a normal good and a luxury (income elastic)."}}

calculations.title: Price elasticity of supply (PES)
formulas: PES = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP
calculations.meaning: How responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price. PES is positive: > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic.
calculations.tip: Same shape as PED, but supply moves with price — so PES is positive, no sign to drop.

practice.question: The price of a good {{s > 0 ? "rises" : "falls"}} from {{m(p1)}} to {{m(p2)}} and quantity supplied changes from {{q1}} to {{q2}} units. Calculate PES and state whether supply is price elastic or price inelastic.
steps: PES is {{pes > 1 ? "greater" : "less"}} than 1, so supply is {{pes > 1 ? "price elastic" : "price inelastic"}}.

calculations.title: Equilibrium from linear demand and supply functions
formulas: Qd = a − bP
Qs = c + dP
At equilibrium Qd = Qs → P* = (a − c) ÷ (b + d)
calculations.meaning: Solves for the market-clearing price and quantity. Substitute P* back into either function to get Q*.
calculations.tip: "Set them equal, collect the P's." Then check Q* in BOTH equations — they must match.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity.

calculations.title: Consumer and producer surplus
formulas: CS = ½ × Q* × (price where Qd = 0 − P*)
PS = ½ × Q* × (P* − price where Qs = 0)
calculations.meaning: Both surpluses are triangles on a linear diagram. Find the price-axis intercepts by setting each function to zero.
calculations.tip: Triangle = ½ × base × height. Base is always Q*; height is the gap between P* and the intercept.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. Calculate consumer surplus and producer surplus at the equilibrium.
steps: Demand meets the price axis where Qd = 0: P = {{a}} ÷ {{b}} = {{m(pmax)}}
Supply meets the price axis where Qs = 0: P = {{f(-c)}} ÷ {{d}} = {{m(pmn)}}

calculations.title: Price ceiling: shortage
formulas: Shortage = Qd − Qs at the maximum price
calculations.meaning: Substitute the maximum price into both functions; the gap between them is the excess demand.
calculations.tip: Ceiling → plug Pmax into BOTH equations. Demand side bigger = shortage.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. The government sets a maximum price of {{m(pc)}}. Calculate quantity demanded, quantity supplied and the shortage.
steps: Equilibrium: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c,d)}} → {{f(a-c)}} = {{b+d}}P → P* = {{m(Pstar)}}, Q* = {{a}} − {{b}} × {{Pstar}} = {{qs}} — the ceiling is below P*, so it is binding.

calculations.title: Price floor: surplus and cost to government
formulas: Surplus = Qs − Qd at the minimum price
Cost of buying the surplus = surplus × minimum price
calculations.meaning: If the government buys the surplus to maintain the floor, it pays the minimum price for every surplus unit.
calculations.tip: Floor → plug Pmin into both equations. Gov. spending = the rectangle: surplus × Pmin.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. The government sets a minimum price of {{m(pf)}} and buys any surplus. Calculate the surplus and the cost to the government.
steps: Equilibrium: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c,d)}} → {{f(a-c)}} = {{b+d}}P → P* = {{m(Pstar)}}, Q* = {{a}} − {{b}} × {{Pstar}} = {{qs}} — the floor is above P*, so it is binding.

calculations.title: Specific tax: prices, quantity, revenue and incidence
formulas: With a tax of t per unit, producers receive P − t: Qs = c + d(P − t)
Tax revenue = t × new Q
Consumer share = (Pc − P*) × new Q
calculations.meaning: The tax shifts supply up by t. Solve the new equilibrium for the price consumers pay; producers keep that price minus the tax.
calculations.tip: "Replace P with (P − t) in supply only." Pc − Pp must always equal the tax.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. The government imposes a specific tax of {{m(t)}} per unit. Calculate the price consumers pay, the price producers receive, the new quantity, the tax revenue and the amount of that revenue paid by consumers.
steps: Before the tax: Equilibrium: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c,d)}} → {{f(a-c)}} = {{b+d}}P → P* = {{m(Pstar)}}, Q* = {{a}} − {{b}} × {{Pstar}} = {{qs}}
Producers now receive P − {{t}}, so supply becomes Qs = {{f(c)}} + {{d}}(P − {{t}}) = {{lin(c - d*t, d)}}
Set equal: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c - d*t, d)}} → {{f(a - c + d*t)}} = {{b+d}}P → Pc = {{m(pc)}}

calculations.title: Welfare loss from a tax
formulas: Welfare loss = ½ × tax per unit × (Q* − new Q)
calculations.meaning: The deadweight triangle between the old and new quantities: its height is the tax, its base is the fall in quantity.
calculations.tip: Height = tax (the vertical gap Pc − Pp), base = lost quantity. Half of base × height.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. A specific tax of {{m(t)}} per unit is imposed, and the new equilibrium quantity is {{q2}} units. Calculate the welfare loss.
steps: Before the tax: Equilibrium: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c,d)}} → {{f(a-c)}} = {{b+d}}P → P* = {{m(Pstar)}}, Q* = {{a}} − {{b}} × {{Pstar}} = {{qs}}

calculations.title: Subsidy: prices, quantity and cost
formulas: With a subsidy of s per unit, producers receive P + s: Qs = c + d(P + s)
Cost to government = s × new Q
calculations.meaning: The subsidy shifts supply down by s. Consumers pay less, producers receive the consumer price plus the subsidy.
calculations.tip: "Replace P with (P + s) in supply." Pp − Pc must equal the subsidy.

practice.question: Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}}, where P is the price in $ and Q is in units. The government pays producers a subsidy of {{m(s)}} per unit. Calculate the price consumers pay, the price producers receive, the new quantity and the cost of the subsidy.
steps: Before the subsidy: Equilibrium: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c,d)}} → {{f(a-c)}} = {{b+d}}P → P* = {{m(Pstar)}}, Q* = {{a}} − {{b}} × {{Pstar}} = {{qs}}
Producers receive P + {{s}}, so supply becomes Qs = {{f(c)}} + {{d}}(P + {{s}}) = {{lin(c + d*s, d)}}
Set equal: {{lin(a,-b)}} = {{lin(c + d*s, d)}} → {{f(a - c - d*s)}} = {{b+d}}P → Pc = {{m(pc)}}

calculations.title: Average and marginal costs
formulas: AFC = TFC ÷ Q
AVC = TVC ÷ Q
ATC = TC ÷ Q = AFC + AVC
MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ
calculations.meaning: Averages divide a total by output; marginal cost is the change in total cost per extra unit.
calculations.tip: Average = total ÷ Q. Marginal = change ÷ change. Fixed costs never affect MC.

practice.question: A firm has total fixed costs of {{m(tfc)}}. At {{q1}} units of output its total variable cost is {{m(tvc1)}}; at {{q2}} units it is {{m(tvc2)}}. Calculate AFC, AVC and ATC at {{q1}} units, and the marginal cost per unit of increasing output from {{q1}} to {{q2}}.

calculations.title: Total, average and marginal revenue
formulas: TR = P × Q
AR = TR ÷ Q = P
MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ
calculations.meaning: For a firm facing downward-sloping demand, MR is below price because the lower price applies to all units sold.
calculations.tip: AR is just the price. MR = change in TR per extra unit — it can be negative.

practice.question: A firm sells {{q1}} units at {{m(p1)}} each. To sell {{q2}} units it must lower its price to {{m(p2)}}. Calculate total revenue at each output and the marginal revenue per unit.
steps: MR = ({{m(tr2)}} − {{m(tr1)}}) ÷ ({{q2}} − {{q1}}) = {{m(mr)}} per unit — below the new price of {{m(p2)}}.

calculations.title: Profit, normal profit and loss
formulas: Economic profit = TR − TC = (AR − ATC) × Q
calculations.meaning: Economic costs include normal profit, so zero economic profit is normal profit; positive is abnormal profit; negative is a loss.
calculations.tip: (P − ATC) × Q. Positive → abnormal, zero → normal, negative → loss.

practice.question: A firm sells {{q}} units at a price of {{m(p)}}. Its average total cost (including normal profit) at this output is {{m(atc)}}. Calculate total revenue, total cost and economic profit, and state what the firm is earning.

parts.label: The firm earns
parts.answer: prof > 0 ? "abnormal profit" : prof === 0 ? "normal profit" : "an economic loss"

steps: {{prof > 0 ? "AR > ATC: abnormal profit." : prof === 0 ? "AR = ATC: normal profit only." : "AR < ATC: an economic loss."}}

calculations.title: GDP by the expenditure approach
formulas: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
calculations.meaning: Adds all spending on final goods and services produced in the country. Net exports can be negative.
calculations.tip: "CIG-XM": Consumption, Investment, Government, eXports minus iMports.

practice.question: An economy has consumption of {{m(C)}}bn, investment of {{m(I)}}bn, government spending of {{m(G)}}bn, exports of {{m(X)}}bn and imports of {{m(M)}}bn. Calculate net exports and GDP.

calculations.title: GNI from GDP
formulas: GNI = GDP + income earned abroad by residents − income earned domestically by foreigners
calculations.meaning: GNI measures the income of a country's residents wherever it is earned: GDP plus net primary income from abroad.
calculations.tip: GDP is WHERE it's made; GNI is WHO earns it. Add income in, subtract income out.

practice.question: A country's GDP is {{m(gdp)}}bn. Its residents earn {{m(inc)}}bn in profits, interest and wages from abroad, while foreign owners of factors earn {{m(out)}}bn in the country. Calculate GNI.

calculations.title: Real GDP using a price deflator
formulas: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price deflator × 100
Real growth = (real GDP₂ − real GDP₁) ÷ real GDP₁ × 100
calculations.meaning: Removes the effect of price changes so you can compare output over time. In the base year the deflator is 100.
calculations.tip: "Divide by the deflator, times 100." Real growth is always smaller than nominal growth when prices rise.

practice.question: In year 1 (the base year, deflator = 100) nominal GDP is {{m(n1)}}bn. In year 2 nominal GDP is {{m(n2)}}bn and the GDP deflator is {{def2}}. Calculate real GDP in year 2 and the real growth rate.
steps: Year 1 is the base year, so real GDP₁ = nominal GDP₁ = {{m(n1)}}bn
Nominal growth was {{f((n2 - n1)/n1*100)}}%, but most of that {{rg > 0 ? "was" : "came from"}} rising prices.

calculations.title: GDP per capita
formulas: GDP per capita = GDP ÷ population
calculations.meaning: Average output (income) per person — a better guide to living standards than total GDP.
calculations.tip: Watch the units: $bn ÷ millions of people = thousands of $ per person.

practice.question: A country has GDP of {{m(gdp)}}bn and a population of {{pop}} million. Calculate GDP per capita.

calculations.title: Economic growth rate
formulas: Growth rate = (real GDP₂ − real GDP₁) ÷ real GDP₁ × 100
calculations.meaning: The percentage change in real GDP. A negative rate means real output fell; two negative quarters is a recession.
calculations.tip: Use REAL GDP. A falling growth rate that is still positive means the economy is still growing.

practice.question: Real GDP rises from {{m(r1)}}bn to {{m(r2)}}bn. Calculate the economic growth rate.

calculations.title: Unemployment rate
formulas: Labour force = employed + unemployed
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
calculations.meaning: The share of people who are willing and able to work and actively seeking work, but have no job.
calculations.tip: Divide by the LABOUR FORCE, not the population — people not seeking work are not in it.

practice.question: In a country {{f(emp)}} thousand people are employed and {{f(un)}} thousand are unemployed and actively seeking work. Calculate the labour force and the unemployment rate.

calculations.title: Inflation rate from a price index
formulas: Inflation rate = (CPI₂ − CPI₁) ÷ CPI₁ × 100
calculations.meaning: The percentage change in the consumer price index. A negative result is deflation; a lower but positive result is disinflation.
calculations.tip: CPI 120 → 126 is 5%, not 6 — divide by the earlier index, not 100.

practice.question: The consumer price index rises from {{f(c1, 2)}} to {{f(c2, 2)}}. Calculate the rate of inflation.

calculations.title: Weighted price index
formulas: Price index for each item = current price ÷ base-year price × 100
CPI = Σ (weight × item index) ÷ Σ weights
calculations.meaning: Items that take a larger share of spending get a larger weight, so they affect measured inflation more.
calculations.tip: Index each item first, then weight-average the indices. In the base year CPI = 100.

practice.question: A basket has three items. Food (weight {{w1}}%) cost {{m(b1)}} in the base year and {{m(n1)}} now; transport (weight {{w2}}%) cost {{m(b2)}} and now {{m(n2)}}; housing (weight {{w3}}%) cost {{m(b3)}} and now {{m(n3)}}. Calculate the weighted price index and the rate of inflation since the base year.
steps: The base year is 100, so prices rose by {{f(cpi - 100)}}%.

calculations.title: Real interest rate
formulas: Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − inflation rate
calculations.meaning: The return on saving (or cost of borrowing) after allowing for inflation. It can be negative.
calculations.tip: "Real = nominal minus inflation." Negative real rates reward borrowers and punish savers.

practice.question: A bank pays a nominal interest rate of {{f(nom)}}% a year and the inflation rate is {{f(inf)}}%. Calculate the real interest rate.
steps: {{real < 0 ? "The real rate is negative: savings lose purchasing power, which encourages spending and borrowing." : "Savers gain purchasing power of " + f(real) + "% a year."}}

calculations.title: The Keynesian multiplier
formulas: Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPW
MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM
ΔReal GDP = multiplier × change in injection
calculations.meaning: An injection becomes income for others, who spend part of it, so the final rise in real GDP is a multiple of the injection.
calculations.tip: "One over the leaks." The more leaks out (S, T, M), the smaller the multiplier.

practice.question: In an economy the marginal propensity to save is {{f(mps)}}, to tax {{f(mpt)}} and to import {{f(mpm)}}. The government increases spending by {{m(dG)}}bn. Calculate the MPC, the multiplier and the eventual change in real GDP.

calculations.title: Average and marginal tax rates
formulas: Average tax rate = total tax ÷ total income × 100
Marginal tax rate = Δtax ÷ Δincome × 100 (the rate on the next $1)
calculations.meaning: In a progressive system each band's rate applies only to income inside that band, so the average rate is below the top marginal rate.
calculations.tip: Tax each slice separately, then add. Progressive ⇔ marginal rate above the average rate.

practice.question: Income tax is 0% on income up to {{m(t1)}}, {{r1}}% on income from {{m(t1)}} to {{m(t2)}}, and {{r2}}% on income above {{m(t2)}}. A person earns {{m(y)}}. Calculate the tax paid, the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate.
steps: {{y > t2 ? r2 + "% band: " + r2 + "% × (" + m(y) + " − " + m(t2) + ") = " + m(r2/100*(y - t2)) : "Income is below " + m(t2) + ", so nothing is taxed at " + r2 + "%"}}
The next dollar earned is taxed at {{marg}}%, the marginal rate.

calculations.title: Budget balance
formulas: Budget balance = government revenue − government expenditure
As % of GDP = balance ÷ GDP × 100
calculations.meaning: A negative balance is a budget deficit (financed by borrowing); a positive one is a surplus.
calculations.tip: Revenue minus spending: minus sign = deficit. Express it as % of GDP to compare countries.

practice.question: Government revenue is {{m(rev)}}bn and government expenditure is {{m(ex)}}bn. GDP is {{m(gdp)}}bn. Calculate the budget balance and express it as a percentage of GDP.

calculations.title: Government debt-to-GDP ratio
formulas: Debt-to-GDP = government debt ÷ GDP × 100
New debt = old debt + this year's deficit
calculations.meaning: A ratio is used to judge whether debt is sustainable: it can fall even with a deficit if GDP grows fast enough.
calculations.tip: Deficits add to the debt (a flow into a stock). Growth in GDP shrinks the ratio.

practice.question: Government debt is {{m(debt)}}bn and nominal GDP is {{m(gdp)}}bn. Next year the government runs a deficit of {{m(def)}}bn and nominal GDP grows by {{g}}%. Calculate the debt-to-GDP ratio now and next year.

calculations.title: Opportunity cost and comparative advantage
formulas: Opportunity cost of 1 X = units of Y given up ÷ units of X gained
calculations.meaning: The country with the lower opportunity cost of a good has the comparative advantage in it, and should specialise in it.
calculations.tip: "Lower OC wins." Each country has a comparative advantage in exactly one of the two goods (unless the ratios are equal).

practice.question: Using all its resources, Country A can produce {{xa}} tonnes of rice or {{ya}} units of textiles; Country B can produce {{xb}} tonnes of rice or {{yb}} units of textiles. Calculate the opportunity cost of 1 tonne of rice in each country and identify the comparative advantages.

parts.label: OC of 1 tonne of rice in A (units of textiles)
OC of 1 tonne of rice in B (units of textiles)

steps: A: 1 tonne of rice costs {{ya}} ÷ {{xa}} = {{f(oca)}} units of textiles
B: 1 tonne of rice costs {{yb}} ÷ {{xb}} = {{f(ocb)}} units of textiles
{{oca < ocb ? "A" : "B"}} gives up less textiles per tonne of rice, so it has the comparative advantage in rice.
Textiles: 1 unit costs A {{f(xa/ya)}} t of rice and B {{f(xb/yb)}} t — {{oca < ocb ? "B" : "A"}} has the lower opportunity cost, so the comparative advantage in textiles.

calculations.title: Tariff: imports, revenue and welfare loss
formulas: Imports = Qd − Qs at the price
Tariff revenue = tariff × imports after the tariff
Welfare loss = ½ × t × (rise in domestic output) + ½ × t × (fall in consumption)
calculations.meaning: A tariff raises the domestic price from Pw to Pw + t. Domestic output rises, consumption falls, and imports shrink.
calculations.tip: Do everything twice: at Pw and at Pw + t. Revenue is the rectangle in the middle; the two triangles are the welfare loss.

practice.question: Domestic demand and supply are Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}} (P in $, Q in units). The world price is {{m(pw)}}. The government imposes a tariff of {{m(t)}} per unit. Calculate imports before and after the tariff, the tariff revenue and the total welfare loss.
steps: At Pw + t = {{m(pw + t)}}: Qs = {{q3}}; Qd = {{q4}}; imports = {{q4 - q3}}

calculations.title: Import quota: price and quota rent
formulas: With a quota, the price rises until Qd − Qs = quota
Quota rent = (new price − world price) × quota
calculations.meaning: Imports are capped, so the domestic price rises. The gap between the new price and Pw on imported units goes to licence holders, not the government.
calculations.tip: Set Qd − Qs equal to the quota and solve for P. Quota rent = price gap × quota.

practice.question: Domestic demand and supply are Qd = {{lin(a,-b)}} and Qs = {{lin(c,d)}} (P in $, Q in units). The world price is {{m(pw)}}. The government limits imports to {{quota}} units. Calculate the new domestic price, domestic production and the quota rent.
steps: Imports at price P = Qd − Qs = ({{lin(a,-b)}}) − ({{lin(c,d)}}) = {{lin(a - c, -(b + d))}}
Set equal to the quota: {{lin(a - c, -(b + d))}} = {{quota}} → P = {{f(a - c - quota)}} ÷ {{b + d}} = {{m(pq)}}

calculations.title: Converting prices between currencies
formulas: If €1 = $x: price in $ = price in € × x
price in € = price in $ ÷ x
calculations.meaning: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, so conversion is a multiplication or division.
calculations.tip: Ask "is the answer bigger or smaller?" — if €1 buys more than $1, a euro price becomes a bigger dollar number.

practice.question: The exchange rate is €1 = ${{fd(x)}}. Calculate the dollar price of a €{{pe}} jacket and the euro price of a ${{pd}} phone case.

calculations.title: Percentage appreciation and depreciation
formulas: % change in value of € = (new $ per € − old $ per €) ÷ old × 100
Value of $ in € = 1 ÷ ($ per €)
calculations.meaning: If one currency appreciates the other depreciates — but not by the same percentage, because the base changes.
calculations.tip: Flip the rate (1 ÷ rate) to see the other currency. 10% up for one is NOT 10% down for the other.

practice.question: The exchange rate changes from €1 = ${{fd(r1)}} to €1 = ${{fd(r2, 4)}}. Calculate the percentage change in the value of the euro and of the dollar.

calculations.title: Balance of payments accounts
formulas: Current account = trade in goods + trade in services + primary income + secondary income
Current + capital + financial account + errors and omissions = 0
calculations.meaning: A current account deficit must be matched by a surplus on the capital and financial accounts (net inflows of investment or borrowing).
calculations.tip: All the accounts sum to zero. Deficit on the current account ⇒ surplus on the financial account.

derived.ca: gx - gm + sx - sm + pin - pout + sec
derived.fa: -(gx - gm + sx - sm + pin - pout + sec) - ka

practice.question: A country's data ($bn): goods exports {{gx}}, goods imports {{gm}}, service exports {{sx}}, service imports {{sm}}, primary income received {{pin}}, primary income paid {{pout}}, net secondary income {{f(sec)}}, capital account balance {{f(ka)}}. Errors and omissions are zero. Calculate the balance of trade in goods, the current account balance and the financial account balance.
steps: The accounts sum to zero: financial = −(current + capital) = −({{f(ca)}} + {{f(ka)}}) = {{f(fa)}}

calculations.title: Terms of trade
formulas: Terms of trade = index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices × 100
calculations.meaning: Above 100 (or rising) means each unit of exports buys more imports: an improvement. Falling means a deterioration.
calculations.tip: "Exports over imports." Up = improvement, even though it may hurt export volumes.

practice.question: From the base year (both indices = 100), the export price index rises to {{xp}} and the import price index to {{mp}}. Calculate the terms of trade and state whether they have improved or deteriorated.
steps: Base year = 100, so they have {{tot > 100 ? "improved: export prices rose relative to import prices" : "deteriorated: import prices rose relative to export prices"}}.
